title: Lazarus Was Already Dead — Jesus Still Told Them to Move the Stone
paragraphs: Lazarus Was Already Dead — Jesus Still Told Them to Move the Stone
What if the thing you buried is not the thing Jesus has abandoned—and the stone you are protecting is standing between your surrender and what He wants you to see?
There are some prayers you stop praying because eventually the silence becomes too painful.
At first, you prayed with expectation.
Then you prayed with tears.
Then you prayed because you were terrified not to.
Maybe it was your marriage.
Your child.
Your faith.
Your calling.
Your purity.
Your family.
The person you used to be before disappointment hollowed something out inside you.
Maybe nobody even knows it died.
You still go to church.
You still know when to say amen.
You still share verses.
You still tell people, “God is good.”
But there is a tomb somewhere inside your heart that you stopped taking people near.
Because some things hurt differently after you have buried them.
Martha understood.
By the time Jesus stood outside Lazarus’s tomb, there was no medical emergency left.
There was no sickbed.
No final treatment to attempt.
No pulse to recover.
No desperate message left to send.
Lazarus was dead.
John makes that painfully clear. Jesus Himself had already told His disciples plainly, “Lazarus died.” Then, when He finally arrived near Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.
Four days.
And Martha had already spoken the sentence so many wounded believers have whispered in different words:
“Lord, if You had been here...”
That sentence is not atheism.
It is wounded faith.
Martha still calls Him Lord.
She still believes He possesses extraordinary authority.
But she cannot reconcile His love with His timing.
And perhaps that is where this story finds you.
You believe Jesus could have done something.
You just cannot understand why He did not do it when you begged Him.
That distinction matters.
Because some of the deepest crises of faith do not begin when people stop believing God exists.
They begin when people know He exists and cannot understand why the God who loves them allowed something to die.
John tells us something almost unbearable before Lazarus dies: Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus.
And then Jesus delayed.
Those truths stand beside each other in the text.
Love.
Delay.
That destroys one of our most dangerous assumptions—that if Jesus loves us, He must always operate according to the timetable we would choose.
Scripture does not permit that conclusion.
His delay was not evidence of indifference.
And when Jesus finally reached the grieving sisters, He did not stand at a safe theological distance from their sorrow.
Jesus wept.
The One who knew resurrection was minutes away still entered their grief.
Think about that.
Jesus knew Lazarus was coming out...
and Jesus still cried.
Christian hope does not require pretending death does not hurt.
Faith is not emotional anesthesia.
Jesus Christ does not shame Mary for weeping at His feet. He does not tell the mourners that their tears prove insufficient faith.
He weeps.
But then He walks toward the tomb.
And everything becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus does not merely comfort them beside the place of death.
He tells them to open it.
The Greek of John 11:39 is strikingly direct:
“Ἄρατε τὸν λίθον.”
Arate ton lithon.
“Take away the stone.”
The verb ἄρατε is an imperative. Jesus is giving a command. The people standing there cannot give Lazarus life—but they can move what is blocking the tomb.
And Martha immediately objects.
Of course she does.
“Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”
In the Greek text, her words include:
“Κύριε, ἤδη ὄζει...”
Kyrie, ēdē ozei...
“Lord, already he smells...”
This is not a polished church scene anymore.
This is death.
Real death.
A sealed grave.
Decomposition.
Grief with an odor.
Jesus is asking Martha to expose the very thing she has already accepted as irreversible.
And suddenly this ancient tomb feels frighteningly modern.
Because we have stones too.
We put them over places we never want opened again.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The resentment we learned to justify.
The pornography history we keep deleting.
The affair we insist is finished but never confessed.
The bitterness toward the person who wounded us.
The shame from something done to us.
The shame from something done by us.
The secret compromise hidden underneath Christian vocabulary.
The prayer life that quietly died.
The Bible collecting dust while our phone receives hours of our attention.
The marriage that still exists legally but feels buried emotionally.
The child whose rebellion has exhausted every prayer you know how to pray.
The ministry wound that made you suspicious of everyone.
The sin you renamed “struggle” because repentance sounded too expensive.
Stone after stone.
And eventually we become skilled at decorating tombs.
That is the terrifying possibility.
You can become so accustomed to protecting dead places that when Jesus says, “Move the stone,” your first instinct is not hope.
It is embarrassment.
“Lord... it smells in there.”
Lord, You do not understand what You will uncover.
Lord, people will see.
Lord, I buried that for a reason.
Lord, I cannot reopen that memory.
Lord, I cannot confess that.
Lord, I cannot forgive them.
Lord, I cannot admit how far I have fallen.
Lord, what if nothing happens after I move it?
And here we need to be biblically careful.

John 11 is first and foremost a revelation of Jesus Christ. It is not a formula promising that every broken relationship will be restored, every illness healed in this life, every lost opportunity returned, or every earthly tragedy reversed exactly as we desire.
Lazarus’s resurrection is a sign.
It points beyond Lazarus.
Jesus had already told Martha:
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
Not merely, I perform resurrection.
“I am.”
Christian hope ultimately rests not in getting every earthly circumstance resurrected according to our preferences, but in Christ Himself—the Son of God who has authority over sin and death.
That distinction protects this beautiful passage from becoming a prosperity slogan.
Jesus is not promising you that every dream you buried is coming back.
Some things need to remain buried.
Some relationships should not be restored to their former form.
Some doors God closes should stay closed.
Some versions of ourselves should never be resurrected.
The Gospel is far greater than “Jesus will give me my old life back.”
The Gospel announces that sinners who were spiritually dead can receive new life in Christ.
And that is where Lazarus’s tomb begins pointing toward something infinitely greater.
Jesus stands before a dead man and commands life where human beings possess no power to produce it.
After the stone is removed, Jesus prays.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking commands in the Gospel of John:
“Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω.”
Lazare, deuro exō.
“Lazarus, come out.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
“Lazarus, heal yourself.”
“Lazarus, try harder.”
“Lazarus, become worthy.”
“Lazarus, prove you deserve another chance.”
The dead man contributes no power to his resurrection.
Jesus speaks.
Lazarus comes out.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a self-improvement project.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside the tomb shouting motivational advice to corpses.
We need grace.
We need forgiveness.
We need life.

Sin is more serious than bad habits needing adjustment. Scripture describes humanity apart from Christ as dead in trespasses and sins. We cannot boast our way into salvation, perform our way into reconciliation with God, or clean ourselves enough to make the cross unnecessary.
Jesus came because we could not save ourselves.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
The sinless Christ bore judgment for sinners.
He was buried.
And on the third day, the tomb that should have held Him could not.
Lazarus came out of his grave still wrapped in grave clothes and would one day physically die again.
Jesus Christ rose never to die again.
That is the greater glory toward which this sign points.
And there is another detail in John 11 that should stop us.
Jesus could raise Lazarus.
Yet He told other people to move the stone.
Then, after Lazarus emerged, Jesus told them:
“Unbind him, and let him go.”
Jesus alone supplied the resurrection power.
Yet people were commanded to participate obediently in what they actually could do.
That matters.
Moving the stone did not resurrect Lazarus.
Jesus did.
Their obedience did not manufacture the miracle.
Jesus did.
So never turn this passage into “If you just work hard enough, God will perform your miracle.”
That is not the Gospel.
But neither should we use the sovereignty of Christ as an excuse for disobedience.
There are stones Jesus has already told us to move through the clear teaching of Scripture.
Repent.
Confess.
Forgive.
Flee sexual immorality.
Put away deceit.
Love one another.
Care for the vulnerable.
Pray.
Abide in Christ.
Take up your cross.
Follow Him.
You cannot resurrect yourself.
But you can stop defending the stone.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needed.
Stop defending the stone.
Stop explaining why your secret sin deserves one more month.
Stop waiting to feel repentant enough before you repent.
Stop confusing conviction with condemnation.
Stop telling Jesus, “It has been four days,” as though the length of your failure determines the reach of His grace.
Maybe it has been four days.
Maybe four years.
Maybe forty.
Jesus is not intimidated by how long you have been hiding.
But grace is not permission to remain inside the tomb.
Grace calls you out.
There is a counterfeit Christianity that wants Jesus to forgive the old life without ever commanding the old life to surrender.
But the Jesus of Scripture says, “Follow Me.”
The Gospel does not merely change your eternal destination while leaving your allegiance untouched.
Christ saves by grace, and the grace that saves begins transforming the person it saves.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without battles.
Not without stumbling.
But genuinely.
This is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace found him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Grace met him at a cross.
And the cross itself looked like the greatest scandal, defeat, and ending imaginable.
The Messiah crucified.
The disciples scattered.
Hope apparently sealed behind stone.
Then came Sunday.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes stories sin has vandalized and writes redemption across them.
He does not call evil good.
He does not pretend wounds never happened.
He does not erase justice.
He does something far more glorious.
He redeems.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe yours has never left your bedroom.
Maybe nobody knows what you have become.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you are carrying consequences that repentance will not magically remove.
Hear this carefully:
The grace of Jesus Christ is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
The cross exists precisely because sinners need mercy.
Repentance means you stop negotiating with the tomb and turn toward Christ.
You bring Him the truth.
All of it.
The ugly part.
The embarrassing part.
The part you wish you could edit out of your testimony.
And you discover that Jesus already knew what was behind the stone when He called you.
He knew.
That may be the most frightening and beautiful truth in this entire article.
Jesus knew what was inside Lazarus’s tomb before anyone moved the stone.
And Jesus knows what is inside yours.
You are not informing an ignorant Savior when you confess.
You are surrendering to a Savior who already knows.
So perhaps today your prayer does not need impressive language.
Perhaps it sounds like this:
Jesus, I have been hiding.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, I cannot save myself.
Jesus, I believe You died for sinners and rose again.
Jesus, expose what must be exposed.
Remove what must be removed.
Kill what must die.
Heal what You desire to heal.
Teach me to obey You.
Make me Yours.
And if those words exposed something you have kept behind a stone, do not turn this into another emotional article you read, feel, and forget.
Be honest.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that Christians do not have to pretend they have never been in tombs.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
You do not know who is scrolling at 2:17 in the morning.
You do not know whose marriage is collapsing.
Whose secret addiction is winning.
Whose shame has convinced them God could never want them.
Whose finger might stop on the words:
Jesus already knows what is behind your stone.

Not because the post itself possesses power, but because there may come a night when disappointment whispers that God has forgotten you, and you will need to return to John 11 and remember what Scripture actually says.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been praying for to follow too.
It does not.
Not because supporting a ministry contributes anything to your salvation.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased salvation. Grace cannot be bought.
But generosity, Gospel partnership, and helping biblical teaching reach more people can be sincere ways believers choose to glorify God with resources He has entrusted to them.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.

It is helping build a place where conviction does not end in despair, where broken people are pointed toward Christ rather than personalities, and where the answer to human scandal is never self-righteousness but repentance, the cross, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus.
And before you leave, go back in your mind to Bethany one final time.
See Martha standing there.
See the mourners.
See the stone.
Smell the reality nobody wanted exposed.
Hear the scraping as human hands begin moving what had sealed the grave.
Then silence.
Jesus lifts His eyes.
He prays.
And the voice that spoke creation into existence addresses a man who cannot possibly answer.
“Lazarus, come out.”
Then...
movement.
The impossible sound of life inside a place built for death.
A man walks out wearing the evidence of where he has been.
And Jesus says to unbind him.
That is grace.
Not pretending there was never a tomb.
Not pretending Lazarus had never died.
Not rewriting history by denying what happened.
Grace is Jesus Christ entering a story everyone else has already pronounced finished and demonstrating that death itself does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So move whatever stone Scripture is calling you to move.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Ask for help where you cannot fight alone.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
And leave resurrection power where it belongs:
in the hands of Jesus.
Because perhaps the stone you are most afraid to move is covering the very place where you most desperately need to encounter the authority, mercy, and glory of Christ.
The tomb may explain where you have been—but when Jesus calls your name, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
